---
title: "2. k3s Architecture and Installation"
description: "Servers and agents, the control-plane components explained as a school, what k3s bundles, how to install, join and uninstall, and the files that matter."
---

## The problem

The Lemonade Stand now has a container image. Next we need a **cluster**: one or more machines that act as one big computer for containers. Before typing commands we should know which programs make up a cluster, where they run, and where k3s keeps its files. Otherwise every error message will be a mystery.

## Explain it like I'm ten

::: {.callout-tip}
## A cluster is a school

Think of the cluster as a school, and every container as a pupil who needs a seat.

- The **API server** is the **front office**. Every request goes through it: "please enrol three lemonade pupils". It checks who you are and whether you are allowed to ask.
- The **datastore** is the **school notebook**. The office writes down every decision. In k3s this notebook is a small SQLite file by default.
- The **scheduler** is the **seat assigner**. It looks at each new pupil and picks a classroom that has room.
- The **controller manager** is the group of **hall monitors**. Each monitor keeps checking one thing, like "are there still three lemonade pupils?", and fixes it when it is wrong. A thermostat works the same way: it keeps checking the temperature and turns the heater on or off.
- Each **node** is a **classroom**. Its **kubelet** is the **class teacher**. It reads the office's list for that room and makes sure those pupils are really there.
- **containerd** is the teacher's pair of hands. It actually starts and stops containers.
- **kube-proxy** and **Flannel** are the corridors and signposts, so messages reach the right room.
- **CoreDNS** is the school phone book. It turns a name like `lemonade-web` into an address.

In *The Illustrated Children's Guide to Kubernetes*, **Captain Kube** steers a ship made of many rafts lashed together, so from outside it looks like one boat. A cluster is the same: many machines that look like one. In k3s, all the office staff (API server, scheduler and controllers) work in **one room**, a single `k3s` process. That is why it is so easy to set up.
:::

## The concept, precisely

**Server and agent.** A *server* runs `k3s server`. It runs the control plane (API server, scheduler, controller manager), the datastore, *and* the kubelet and container runtime, so it can run pods too. An *agent* runs `k3s agent`. It has only the kubelet, containerd and networking, and it joins a server. One server on its own is already a complete cluster.

**The datastore.**

- **SQLite** (the default) is for a single server. k3s talks to it through a translation layer called **kine**, which makes SQLite look like etcd to Kubernetes.
- **Embedded etcd** is for high availability (HA). You start the first server with `--cluster-init`, and you run an **odd** number of servers, usually 3.
- **External** MySQL, PostgreSQL or etcd is chosen with `--datastore-endpoint`.

**What k3s bundles.** Upstream Kubernetes leaves these choices to you. k3s ships one choice for each, and you can switch any of them off with `--disable`:

| Need | Upstream Kubernetes | k3s default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Container runtime | You install one | containerd (built in) |
| Pod network (CNI) | You install one | Flannel (VXLAN) |
| Cluster DNS | You install one | CoreDNS |
| Ingress controller | None | Traefik v3 |
| `LoadBalancer` Services | Stay `Pending` without a cloud | ServiceLB (formerly Klipper LB) |
| Storage for PVCs | None on bare metal | local-path-provisioner |
| `kubectl top`, autoscaling metrics | Install metrics-server | metrics-server |
| Network policies | Depends on CNI | kube-router's policy controller |
| Helm charts as objects | Not available | Helm controller with the `HelmChart` resource |
| Gateway API definitions | Install yourself | `gateway-api-crd` chart |

The packaged components are deployed from manifest files that k3s writes into `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests`. Each file becomes an **AddOn** object ([lesson 13](13-helm-and-auto-deploy.qmd)).

**How agents join.** An agent opens a connection to a server on port 6443. It proves it is allowed to join with the **join token**, which is stored on the server at `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/node-token`. After that, all kubelet traffic travels through this tunnel, so agents do not need to accept incoming connections from the server.

## Every option and path for this topic

### Install-script environment variables

| Variable | What it does | Rule / convention | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `INSTALL_K3S_VERSION` | Install an exact version | Pin it in automation | `INSTALL_K3S_VERSION=v1.37.2+k3s1` |
| `INSTALL_K3S_CHANNEL` | Pick a release channel | `stable` (default), `latest`, `testing` | `INSTALL_K3S_CHANNEL=stable` |
| `INSTALL_K3S_EXEC` | Command and flags for the service | Defaults to `server`, or `agent` if `K3S_URL` is set | `INSTALL_K3S_EXEC="server --disable=traefik"` |
| `K3S_URL` | Server to join | Setting it makes the node an **agent** | `K3S_URL=https://10.0.0.10:6443` |
| `K3S_TOKEN` | Shared join secret | Copy it from the server's `node-token` file | `K3S_TOKEN=K10…` |
| `K3S_NODE_NAME` | Node name | Must be unique in the cluster | `K3S_NODE_NAME=stand-2` |
| `K3S_KUBECONFIG_MODE` | File mode of the kubeconfig | `644` lets non-root users read it (lab only) | `K3S_KUBECONFIG_MODE=644` |

### Common `k3s server` flags (also keys in `config.yaml`)

| Flag | What it does | Rule / convention | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--disable` | Do not deploy a packaged component | Repeat it, or use a comma list | `--disable=traefik` |
| `--write-kubeconfig-mode` | Permissions of `k3s.yaml` | Keep `600` on real servers | `--write-kubeconfig-mode=644` |
| `--tls-san` | Extra name or IP on the API certificate | Needed to reach the API by a public name | `--tls-san=k3s.example.com` |
| `--node-label` | Label this node at registration | `key=value` | `--node-label=zone=kitchen` |
| `--node-taint` | Taint this node at registration | `key=value:Effect` | `--node-taint=role=db:NoSchedule` |
| `--cluster-init` | Start a new embedded-etcd cluster | Only on the first HA server | `--cluster-init` |
| `--datastore-endpoint` | Use an external database | A connection string | `--datastore-endpoint="mysql://…"` |
| `--default-local-storage-path` | Where local-path volumes live | Put it on a big disk | `--default-local-storage-path=/data` |
| `--secrets-encryption` | Encrypt Secrets at rest | Turn it on for real clusters | `--secrets-encryption` |

### Files and paths

| Path | What it is | Rule / convention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml` | Admin kubeconfig | Copy it to your laptop; change `127.0.0.1` to the server address |
| `/etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml` | Configuration file | Same keys as the CLI flags without `--` |
| `/etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml.d/*.yaml` | Drop-in config files | Loaded in alphabetical order |
| `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/` | Auto-deploy folder | Files here are applied like `kubectl apply` |
| `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/node-token` | Join token | Keep it secret |
| `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/db/` | SQLite or etcd data | Back it up |
| `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/storage/` | local-path volume data | Lost if the node is lost |
| `/usr/local/bin/k3s-uninstall.sh` | Removes a server | Deletes cluster data |
| `/usr/local/bin/k3s-agent-uninstall.sh` | Removes an agent | |
| `/usr/local/bin/k3s-killall.sh` | Stops k3s and all its containers | Use before maintenance |

A configuration file says the same thing as flags, but you can keep it in Git:

```yaml
# /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml
write-kubeconfig-mode: "0644"
disable:
  - traefik
node-label:
  - "zone=kitchen"
```

## Worked example

### Install on Linux

```bash
# server
curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -
sudo cat /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/node-token

# each agent
curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | K3S_URL=https://SERVER_IP:6443 K3S_TOKEN=TOKEN sh -

# remove again (this deletes cluster data)
/usr/local/bin/k3s-uninstall.sh          # on the server
/usr/local/bin/k3s-agent-uninstall.sh    # on an agent
```

The script installs a systemd (or OpenRC) service. It also installs `kubectl`, `crictl`, `ctr`, `k3s-killall.sh` and `k3s-uninstall.sh`.

### Look around the lab cluster

These outputs come from the Docker lab cluster described in the [part index](index.qmd):

```bash
docker exec k3s-lab k3s --version
kubectl get nodes -o wide
```

```text
k3s version v1.37.2+k3s1 (f6973cb8)
NAME      STATUS   ROLES           VERSION        INTERNAL-IP   CONTAINER-RUNTIME
k3s-lab   Ready    control-plane   v1.37.2+k3s1   172.17.0.3    containerd://2.3.7-k3s1
```

One node, with the `control-plane` role, running containerd. No Docker inside.

```bash
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
```

```text
NAME                                      READY   STATUS      RESTARTS
coredns-577d995dff-hk9ft                  1/1     Running     0
helm-install-traefik-7plmh                0/1     Completed   1
helm-install-traefik-crd-s9fpp            0/1     Completed   0
local-path-provisioner-56c6584955-wd8ch   1/1     Running     0
svclb-traefik-c281d43a-6lgfb              2/2     Running     0
traefik-68df944ff7-2t77b                  1/1     Running     0
```

- `coredns` is the phone book.
- `helm-install-traefik` is a one-off Job that the Helm controller used to install Traefik.
- `svclb-traefik` is ServiceLB, publishing Traefik on the node's ports 80 and 443.
- `local-path-provisioner` creates volumes.

(We started this lab with `--disable=metrics-server` to save memory; a default install also shows a `metrics-server` pod.)

There is no `kube-apiserver` or `etcd` pod. They live inside the single `k3s` process. The auto-deploy folder shows where the add-ons come from:

```bash
docker exec k3s-lab ls /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests
kubectl get addons -n kube-system
```

```text
ccm.yaml  coredns.yaml  gateway-api-crd.yaml  local-storage.yaml  rolebindings.yaml  runtimes.yaml  traefik.yaml

NAME              SOURCE
coredns           /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/coredns.yaml
local-storage     /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/local-storage.yaml
traefik           /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/traefik.yaml
...
```

## Rules and conventions

- Use **one server** to learn, and **three servers with embedded etcd** when the control plane must survive a machine failure.
- Give every node a unique host name, or set `K3S_NODE_NAME`.
- Put settings in `/etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml`, not only in install-script variables. Re-running the script without the same variables loses them; the config file stays.
- Never edit the packaged manifests (`traefik.yaml`, `coredns.yaml`). k3s rewrites them at start-up. Customise with `--disable` or a `HelmChartConfig` ([lesson 13](13-helm-and-auto-deploy.qmd)).
- Use the **same critical flags** (for example `--disable` and `--cluster-cidr`) on every server, or the extra servers refuse to join.
- Open port 6443/TCP from agents to servers, 8472/UDP between nodes (Flannel VXLAN), 10250/TCP between nodes (metrics) and 2379–2380/TCP between servers (HA etcd).
- The documented minimum is 2 cores and 2 GB RAM for a server, and 1 core and 512 MB for an agent.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Copying `k3s.yaml` to a laptop unchanged | `connection refused` to `127.0.0.1:6443` | Replace `127.0.0.1` with the server's address |
| Server reached by a name that is not on its certificate | `x509: certificate is valid for …` | Add `--tls-san=<name>` and restart |
| Two machines with the same host name | The second node never becomes `Ready` | Set `K3S_NODE_NAME` or use `--with-node-id` |
| Two HA servers instead of three | Losing one server stops the API | Use an odd number: 3 or 5 |
| Editing `traefik.yaml` in the manifests folder | The change disappears after a restart | Use a `HelmChartConfig` instead |

## Mathematical Abstraction

With embedded etcd, the servers vote. A change is accepted only when a **majority** (the *quorum*) agrees. The k3s documentation states the quorum as $(n/2)+1$, using whole-number division:

$$
q = \left\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right\rfloor + 1, \qquad f = n - q
$$

where

- $n$ is the number of server nodes in the etcd cluster, a whole number $\ge 1$.
- $q$ is the quorum: how many servers must be up and agree. $\lfloor x \rfloor$ means round down.
- $f$ is the number of servers that may fail while the cluster still works.

**Example:**

- $n = 1$: $q = \lfloor 0.5 \rfloor + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1$ and $f = 1 - 1 = 0$. One server cannot lose anything.
- $n = 3$: $q = \lfloor 1.5 \rfloor + 1 = 2$ and $f = 3 - 2 = 1$. One server can fail.
- $n = 4$: $q = \lfloor 2 \rfloor + 1 = 3$ and $f = 4 - 3 = 1$. Still only one, even though you paid for a fourth machine.
- $n = 5$: $q = 3$ and $f = 2$.

This is why HA k3s uses an **odd** number of servers. Going from 3 to 4 adds a machine but no extra tolerance.

The single-server SQLite set-up has $n = 1$ in this sense: if that server is down, nobody can change the cluster. Pods that are already running on agents keep running, though, because each kubelet keeps its last instructions.
